title: How many Labour MPs actually support devolution?
gist: New PM Andy Burnham has made English devolution the organising principle of his premiership, with a 'Number 10 North' presence in Manchester, but 37 per cent of Labour MPs sit in seats with no mayor and those seats have majorities averaging 12.8 per cent versus 22.7 per cent for mayoral seats — so the binding constraint is Westminster self-interest, not Whitehall. Reform UK's arrival has also broken the Conservative assumption that maturing devolution would generate Tory power bases.

insights.claim: Speaking at Manchester's People's History Museum on 29th June, then-incoming prime minister Andy Burnham pledged the most radical transfer of power out of Westminster in modern British history, to be overseen by a permanent Downing Street presence in Manchester dubbed 'Number 10 North'.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: A dedicated Number 10 unit outside London is a concrete institutional commitment — watch its staffing and budget as the real test of intent versus rhetoric, and as a signal for regional infrastructure and planning pipelines.
insights.locator: Burham’s campaign left little doubt about his intentions

insights.claim: No prime minister has placed devolution so squarely at the heart of their administration, and no prime minister apart from Boris Johnson has entered Downing Street with first-hand experience of governing as an elected mayor.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Mayoral experience makes the delivery risk different in kind from previous devolution promises — this is the most credible UK decentralisation attempt in decades.
insights.locator: It’s early days but, so far, Burnham has been different

insights.claim: Whereas the Starmer government appeared intellectually hesitant about the ultimate destination of English devolution, Burnham has embraced it as an organising principle, which may push him toward bold options such as creating a new generation of mayoral authorities across England within the remaining parliament.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: New mayoral combined authorities would create new commissioning bodies with transport, housing and skills budgets — a pipeline for regional contractors and a new set of counterparties for infrastructure finance.
insights.locator: Yet Burnham appears considerably more confident

themes.theme: The Labour parliamentary arithmetic of resistance

insights.claim: More than a third of Labour MPs — 37 per cent — sit in constituencies that are not currently represented by a mayor, giving a large bloc of the governing party no local stake in the devolution settlement.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: A 37 per cent bloc with no institutional interest in devolution is enough to slow or dilute legislation — the number to watch when assessing whether Burnham's programme survives contact with the whips.
insights.quote: More than a third of Labour MPs—37 per cent—have been elected in constituencies that are not currently represented by a mayor.
insights.locator: Our analysis illustrates the challenge facing Burnham

insights.claim: Labour MPs in constituencies with a mayor hold average majorities of 22.7 per cent, while those without a mayor average 12.8 per cent — a ten-point gap that makes the non-mayoral cohort structurally more risk-averse.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Electoral vulnerability correlates with devolution scepticism, so opposition to reform will intensify as the next election approaches rather than fade.
insights.quote: Small majorities make MPs nervous of change.
insights.locator: For MPs representing a constituency with a mayor

insights.claim: The most marginal Labour seats without mayoral representation include the Forest of Dean, won by 278 votes in 2024, and Sittingbourne and Sheppey, won by 355 votes.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Three-figure majorities mean the marginal Labour MP has almost no tolerance for structural change with uncertain local payoff — a hard ceiling on how fast reform can move.
insights.locator: Among them are razor-thin marginals

insights.claim: Many Labour MPs support devolution in principle but are considerably more cautious in private, because powerful mayors shift influence away from Westminster and can become future political rivals or divert attention from national politics.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Public support and private resistance means announced consensus is not predictive — track committee-stage amendments and boundary decisions rather than public statements.
insights.locator: Many Labour MPs are supportive of devolution in principle

insights.claim: Labour governments have a history of centralising tendencies, and what administrations say on taking power can change in the face of a need to 'grip' priorities from the centre.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: The base case for Labour devolution promises is partial retreat under delivery pressure — price in slippage on any devolved funding settlement.
insights.locator: On the left, objections have taken on a different tone

themes.theme: Reform UK broke the Conservative devolution calculation

insights.claim: The Conservative party advanced English devolution through the last decade in the knowledge that the largest new combined authorities would elect Labour mayors, betting that as devolution matured into market towns and rural England, new Conservative power bases would emerge.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Understanding the original partisan bargain explains why Conservative support could now be withdrawn — the payoff they were promised has been captured by someone else.
insights.locator: This scepticism is, of course, not a uniquely Labour phenomenon

insights.claim: Reform UK has disrupted the Conservative bet on devolution: the Conservatives and Reform now each hold two mayoralties, meaning England's mayor-led strategic authorities will not resolve into an old Labour-versus-Conservative contest.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Multi-party mayoral geography raises policy variance across English regions — regional regulatory and planning risk becomes idiosyncratic rather than nationally correlated.
insights.locator: Reform UK has disrupted that assumption

insights.claim: Polling shows Reform and the Greens outperforming the Conservatives in the Greater Manchester race to replace Burnham as mayor.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: The Greater Manchester succession is a near-term read on whether Reform and the Greens can win metropolitan executive office — a bellwether for the next general election's fragmentation.
insights.locator: Indeed, there is polling showing that Reform and the Greens

insights.claim: Conservative mayors Andy Street and Ben Houchen showed that Conservatives could win in areas assumed to be Labour strongholds, which was the empirical basis for the Conservative devolution strategy.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Mayoral incumbency has a strong personal-vote component that decouples from national polling — relevant when forecasting who controls regional investment budgets.
insights.locator: Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region and South Yorkshire

insights.claim: A YouGov survey of Welsh and Scottish voters conducted ahead of the 2026 Senedd election found 58 per cent of Conservative voters supported abolishing devolution in Scotland, rising in Wales to 66 per cent of Conservative voters and 61 per cent of Reform voters.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Majority abolitionist sentiment among right-of-centre voters makes devolved institutions a live constitutional risk under a future right-leaning government, which matters for the durability of devolved fiscal and planning powers.
insights.locator: Available polling on devolution shows a similarly complex picture

insights.claim: Reform UK was forced to rule out abolishing the Senedd after one of its own politicians publicly floated the idea, showing the party has not fully resolved its position on devolved institutions.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Reform's stated commitments on devolution are unstable — treat them as a source of headline risk for Welsh and Scottish policy continuity.
insights.locator: Reform was ultimately forced to rule out abolishing the Senedd

insights.claim: The right's historical objection to devolution is that it adds a tier of government, red tape and bureaucracy while fragmenting national decision-making — a lineage running from Margaret Thatcher's abolition of the Greater London Council through John Major's opposition to Scottish and Welsh devolution to Conservative scepticism of the Greater London Authority and regional assemblies.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: There is precedent for outright abolition of a devolved English institution, so 'institutions are permanent' assumptions should be stress-tested.
insights.locator: The right has long questioned devolution

insights.claim: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded to Burnham's plans by telling GB News that devolution is just a process that does not in itself fix any problems, an argument likely to grow louder as more powers, funding and influence leave Westminster.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: The opposition is positioning against devolution as delivery-irrelevant rather than as constitutionally wrong — a lower-cost attack line that could gain traction if regional outcomes disappoint.
insights.quote: devolution is just a process; it doesn’t, in and of itself, fix any problems.
insights.locator: In response to Burnham’s plans, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch

insights.claim: Embedding devolution is strategically astute precisely because institutions once established develop their own legitimacy, expectations and democratic mandates, making outright abolition politically difficult even if future governments amend them.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Institutional creation is a ratchet: new mayoral authorities established this parliament are likely to persist across changes of government, which raises the confidence with which long-dated regional commitments can be underwritten.
insights.quote: Institutions, once established, develop their own legitimacy.
insights.locator: Embedding further devolution in the UK

insights.claim: The paradox of the devolution agenda is that the more successfully power is redistributed away from Westminster, the more resistance it generates from those losing influence — so Burnham's greatest obstacle is Westminster politics rather than Whitehall bureaucracy.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Watch the parliamentary Labour party, not the civil service, for the signal on whether devolution legislation passes intact.
insights.quote: Burnham may well discover that his greatest obstacle is not Whitehall bureaucracy but Westminster politics.
insights.locator: As devolution matures, those different strands of scepticism

insights.claim: The decade-long broad consensus that the UK was headed toward more devolution could now fray, shifting the central argument from who should wield power and how to whether the UK government should devolve power at all.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: A shift to existential debate about devolution itself would inject constitutional uncertainty into UK regional policy — a new risk factor for long-horizon regional investment.
insights.locator: Could his premiership mark the beginning of an era

insights.claim: The remaining devolution decisions — over mayoral governance and the boundaries of new strategic authorities — are inherently political and will create winners and losers both between parties and within them.
insights.speaker: Jack Shaw, Dylan Cridland
insights.so_what: Boundary-setting is where the value accrues or is lost for specific regions — the practical detail investors in local infrastructure should track most closely.
insights.locator: The difficult decisions still to come
